opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few layers to it.

The first is simply scale and cost. In language or vision, the internet handed us an enormous, almost free corpus. In embodied work, every trajectory has to be physically produced — someone teleoperating a robot, a real arm moving in a real room, things breaking, resets taking time. So when people said "we'll just collect a lot of data and the scaling story will repeat," they underestimated how slow and expensive each unit of data actually is. You can spend months and end up with what, in token terms, looks tiny.

The second is diversity, which I'd argue matters more than raw volume. A lot of early datasets were collected in a handful of labs, on a few robot bodies, with fairly repetitive tasks — pick this, place that, open the drawer. The models learned those setups very well, but the moment you change the lighting, the table, the object, or the embodiment, performance drops off. So the data looked big on paper but was actually quite narrow in distribution. Volume without coverage doesn't give you generalization.

Third, there's a mismatch between what we record and what the model actually needs. We log joint angles, camera frames, maybe some language instruction. But a lot of what makes manipulation work — force, contact, subtle tactile feedback, the intent behind a correction — is either missing or very noisy. Teleoperation data also carries the operator's habits and hesitations, so you're partly imitating human quirks rather than clean, optimal behavior.

And finally, I think the field has been a bit too optimistic that "embodied-native" data alone would carry everything. In practice, the knowledge about how the world looks and behaves — physics, object permanence, what things are for — is largely already present in video and in large pretrained models. If you insist on learning all of that from scratch through robot trajectories, you're asking a very expensive data source to do a job that cheaper sources could do much better.

So my view is that real-robot data is still essential, but its role should be narrower and sharper: grounding, alignment to a specific body, closing the last gap. The broad understanding of the world should come from somewhere richer — video, simulation, world models — and then the embodied data tells the system how *this* body actually acts in it. When people expected the embodied data to do both jobs at once, that's where it fell short.

r001.rationale: The response discusses embodied-data cost, diversity, and coverage, but does not suggest that projects before the embodied-native push that lacked a foundation model may not have needed much data.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we borrowed the wrong mental model from language and vision, and the data problem in embodied AI is just structurally different.

In NLP, the data already existed. Humanity spent decades writing the internet, and the labs just scraped it. Vision was similar: billions of images with captions, essentially free. So "scaling" there meant scaling compute and model size against a corpus that was already sitting there. Embodied work doesn't have that. There is no internet of robot trajectories. Every sample has to be produced by a physical system interacting with the physical world, which means every sample costs time, hardware, and often a human operator. So when people said "we just need to scale data," they were importing an assumption that didn't hold.

The second issue is that even the data we do collect is much lower quality than it looks. Teleoperation data is the dominant source right now, and it has a few problems. The operator's behavior is not optimal, it's not consistent across sessions, and it's heavily biased toward the specific setup: this table, this lighting, this gripper, this camera placement. So you get a dataset that's large in count but very narrow in distribution. The model memorizes the setup rather than learning the skill. You change the table height by five centimeters and the policy falls apart. That's not a data quantity failure, it's a diversity failure, and diversity is much more expensive to buy than volume.

Third, I think there's a confusion about what the data is supposed to teach. In language, the supervision is dense: every token is a prediction target and the signal is rich. In manipulation, the actual information content of a demonstration is quite sparse. Most of a trajectory is uninformative motion, and the critical moments, like the instant of contact or grasp, are a tiny fraction of the frames. So you need enormous amounts of raw data to get a small amount of useful signal, and nobody fully worked that into their expectations.

And then there's the simulation and video shortcut. A lot of people hoped we could escape the cost by generating data in simulation or by learning from human videos. Both help, but neither has closed the gap. Sim-to-real still leaks, especially for contact-rich tasks, and human video gives you intent and rough kinematics but not the force, the tactile feedback, or the embodiment-specific control that actually matters at execution time.

So my view is that data hasn't "fallen short" so much as our framing was off. The question shouldn't be how many hours we've collected. It should be how much of the relevant task and environment distribution we've actually covered, and what representation makes each sample go further. I'd rather have a smaller dataset designed around that than another million episodes of the same tabletop pick-and-place.

r001.rationale: The response says embodied AI needs costly physical data and that prior scaling assumptions were mistaken. It does not suggest that projects outside the push for embodied-native foundation models may not have needed much data.

astra-6.text:
I think part of the problem is that we expect the amount of data to tell us how much progress we should get. But in embodied intelligence, an hour of data can mean very different things. If a robot repeats the same successful motion in the same environment, you can collect a lot of hours without adding much information about how to handle a new situation.

And the data is tied to the system that produced it: the robot’s body, its sensors, its action space. Two datasets may look similar visually but require very different actions. So simply putting them together doesn’t necessarily produce a more general capability.

There’s also a mismatch between demonstrations and deployment. Demonstrations show what to do when things go well. A deployed robot needs to recognize when something has gone wrong and recover. If those situations are missing from the data, collecting more clean demonstrations may not solve the problem.

So I wouldn’t conclude that data has failed. I’d say we still need a better loop between collecting data, training the model, and testing it in the world. The question is less ‘How many hours do we have?’ and more ‘What does the robot still fail at, and what data would help it learn that?’

r001.rationale: The response discusses why more data may not improve embodied intelligence, but it does not say that earlier projects without foundation models may not have needed much data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main issue is that we’ve confused the amount of data with the amount of useful learning signal. In embodied work, a video can show you what happened, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you what action was taken, what force was applied, or why that action succeeded. Those distinctions matter when a model has to act in the physical world.

The data is also fragmented across different robots, sensors, environments, and control systems. An action on one robot doesn’t automatically mean the same thing on another. So collecting more trajectories doesn’t always produce the kind of transferable improvement people expect.

And much of the data captures successful demonstrations. But an embodied system needs to recognize mistakes, recover from them, and deal with situations outside the demonstration. My view is that we need a tighter loop between collecting data, training a policy, testing it, and collecting the specific experiences that expose its weaknesses. Scale matters, but the learning loop has to make that scale useful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses why more data may not yield useful or transferable learning in embodied work, but it does not say that earlier projects without foundation models may not have needed much data.
